title: GERD: Typical Symptoms First, Alarm Features Change the Path
bottomLine: Typical heartburn/regurgitation without alarm features can often be managed clinically with lifestyle measures and an appropriate acid-suppression trial. Dysphagia, GI bleeding, anemia, weight loss, persistent vomiting or refractory symptoms require diagnostic evaluation rather than indefinite empiric PPI escalation.
recognize: Heartburn and regurgitation are typical; chronic cough, chest discomfort or laryngeal symptoms are less specific and should not be attributed to reflux automatically.
Nocturnal/positional symptoms and meal-related regurgitation support reflux but do not exclude cardiac disease when chest pain is concerning.
differentiate: ACS, esophageal obstruction, eosinophilic esophagitis, peptic ulcer disease and functional dyspepsia can mimic reflux symptoms.
Barrett's-esophagus screening is risk-based and is not indicated for every person with occasional reflux.
assessment: Assess symptom pattern, dysphagia/odynophagia, bleeding/anemia, weight change, NSAIDs, pregnancy, tobacco/alcohol, meal timing, obesity and medication triggers.
workup: Use upper endoscopy for alarm features, treatment-refractory disease or specific Barrett/structural indications.
Ambulatory reflux monitoring and manometry are reserved for unresolved diagnostic questions and specialty pathways rather than routine initial testing.
management: Use health-behaviour measures that fit the patient's triggers and an evidence-based PPI course when indicated; step down to the lowest effective strategy when symptoms are controlled and no long-term indication requires continuous high-dose therapy.
Treat complications such as erosive esophagitis/stricture/Barrett according to GI guidance.
medicationSafety: Do not stop a clearly indicated PPI solely because of nonspecific observational safety concerns, but avoid indefinite therapy without confirming an ongoing indication.
Review NSAIDs/antiplatelets and drug interactions when bleeding or ulcer risk exists.
counselling: Explain that PPIs work best when taken correctly and that lifestyle advice should be individualized rather than a long universal prohibition list.
followUp: Reassess response and indication after the initial course; persistent/recurrent alarm symptoms need diagnostic evaluation.
examTrap: Increasing PPI indefinitely in a patient with progressive dysphagia and weight loss instead of arranging endoscopic evaluation.
oneLinePearl: Typical reflux can be treated empirically; alarm features turn reflux symptoms into a diagnostic problem.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology upper-GI practice resources
Choosing Wisely Canada gastroenterology/primary-care stewardship principles

title: Peptic Ulcer and H. pylori: Diagnose the Cause and Confirm Eradication
bottomLine: Peptic ulcer disease is commonly related to H. pylori or ulcerogenic medications. Test for active H. pylori with an appropriate method, treat using the current locally effective regimen rather than a memorized obsolete combination, remove avoidable NSAID exposure and confirm eradication after treatment.
recognize: Epigastric pain, nausea or dyspepsia can occur, but ulcer disease may present first with bleeding/perforation.
H. pylori infection may be asymptomatic and is linked to ulcer recurrence and gastric malignancy risk.
differentiate: Serology can remain positive after prior infection and is less useful for proving active infection or cure than urea-breath/stool antigen testing in the appropriate setting.
NSAID ulcer disease and H. pylori can coexist; finding one does not eliminate the other.
assessment: Ask about melena/hematemesis, NSAIDs/ASA/steroids/anticoagulants, prior H. pylori treatment, antibiotic/macrolide exposure, smoking, pregnancy and alarm symptoms.
workup: Use urea breath or stool antigen testing for active infection when appropriate, accounting for PPI/antibiotic/bismuth effects on test accuracy; use endoscopy when bleeding, alarm features, age/risk or refractory disease requires it.
Obtain biopsy-based testing when endoscopy is already indicated.
management: Use a current regional/Canadian eradication regimen informed by prior antibiotic exposure and resistance patterns; provide acid suppression and stop avoidable ulcerogenic drugs.
Confirm eradication after therapy using a validated active-infection test at the appropriate post-treatment interval rather than assuming symptom resolution equals cure.
medicationSafety: Do not reuse failed clarithromycin-based therapy reflexively when prior macrolide exposure/resistance makes success unlikely.
Balance NSAID/antiplatelet need against bleeding risk and use gastroprotection when an ongoing indication remains.
counselling: Explain why eradication testing matters even when pain improves and review medication adherence for the full regimen.
followUp: Document cure and reassess persistent symptoms, ulcer healing or malignancy risk according to the endoscopic diagnosis.
examTrap: Calling H. pylori eradicated because symptoms resolved or using an old standard regimen without considering prior antibiotics and local resistance.
oneLinePearl: Treat the organism with a current regimen, then prove it is gone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology H. pylori and dyspepsia resources

title: Dyspepsia: Alarm Features, H. pylori, Then Symptom-Directed Care
bottomLine: Dyspepsia is upper-abdominal pain/burning, early satiety or postprandial fullness—not a diagnosis of ulcer or reflux. Assess alarm/cancer risk, use H. pylori test-and-treat and/or a PPI strategy according to the Canadian pathway, and reserve endoscopy for patients whose age/risk/alarm or refractory course makes it useful.
recognize: Functional dyspepsia is common after structural disease is reasonably excluded; symptom severity does not reliably predict ulcer disease.
Biliary, pancreatic, cardiac and medication causes may mimic dyspepsia.
differentiate: Predominant reflux symptoms are managed as GERD; progressive dysphagia/weight loss/bleeding require structural evaluation.
H. pylori treatment is different from empiric acid suppression and requires eradication confirmation when infection is treated.
assessment: Assess bleeding/anemia, dysphagia, vomiting, weight loss, family/cancer risk, NSAIDs, H. pylori history, pregnancy, alcohol and cardiopulmonary symptoms.
workup: Use noninvasive H. pylori testing where appropriate and endoscopy according to age/risk/alarm and treatment response.
Avoid broad imaging/lab panels unless the symptom pattern suggests another organ system.
management: Treat H. pylori when present; use a time-limited PPI trial for appropriate H. pylori-negative/persistent dyspepsia and consider functional-dyspepsia therapies when structural disease is excluded.
Address NSAIDs and diet/meal triggers without imposing unsupported restrictive diets.
medicationSafety: Avoid indefinite dose escalation without reassessing diagnosis and indication.
Consider pregnancy, bleeding risk and interactions before symptom medications.
counselling: Explain that symptoms may persist despite normal endoscopy because functional dyspepsia is a real gut-brain disorder, not 'nothing wrong'.
followUp: Reassess response after the planned trial and investigate new alarm features rather than continuing empiric therapy indefinitely.
examTrap: Ordering endoscopy for every young low-risk patient with uncomplicated dyspepsia before using the recommended initial strategy.
oneLinePearl: Dyspepsia is managed by risk first, H. pylori second, and symptom phenotype after that.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Dyspepsia Guideline

title: Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Confirm Inflammation, Define Extent, Treat to Control Disease
bottomLine: Crohn disease and ulcerative colitis are chronic inflammatory diseases confirmed from clinical, endoscopic, histologic and imaging evidence. Separate inflammatory activity from infection and IBS-like symptoms, define disease extent/severity and use steroid-sparing maintenance therapy rather than repeating corticosteroid courses without a long-term plan.
recognize: Bloody diarrhea/urgency can suggest colitis; Crohn disease can cause abdominal pain, weight loss, fistula/perianal disease or obstructive symptoms.
Extraintestinal arthritis, skin, eye and hepatobiliary disease can accompany IBD.
differentiate: Enteric infection, C. difficile, ischemia, celiac disease and functional symptoms can mimic IBD activity.
Persistent IBS-like symptoms can occur even when objective inflammation is controlled; escalating immunosuppression without evidence of inflammation can harm.
assessment: Assess stool frequency/blood, pain, fever, weight/nutrition, perianal disease, extraintestinal symptoms, smoking, pregnancy, medications, infection exposure and prior biologic response.
workup: Use CBC, inflammatory markers, stool infection testing and fecal calprotectin when appropriate, followed by colonoscopy/ileoscopy with biopsy and cross-sectional imaging according to disease location/severity.
Before advanced immunosuppression, complete infection/vaccine screening required by the drug/class.
management: Treat according to Crohn/UC location and severity using current GI specialty guidance; minimize repeated systemic steroid exposure and use effective maintenance therapy.
Severe acute colitis, toxic megacolon, abscess, obstruction/perforation or major bleeding requires hospital/surgical/GI escalation.
medicationSafety: Biologic/small-molecule therapy requires infection, vaccination, pregnancy and class-specific lab monitoring.
NSAIDs may exacerbate disease in some patients and should be reviewed when symptoms worsen.
counselling: Teach medication adherence, smoking cessation for Crohn disease, vaccination/infection precautions and the difference between inflammatory flare and functional symptoms.
followUp: Use objective disease-control targets, nutrition and colorectal-cancer surveillance according to duration/extent/risk rather than symptoms alone.
examTrap: Giving another steroid burst for diarrhea in a biologic-treated patient without checking infection or objective inflammation.
oneLinePearl: In IBD, prove the inflammation before escalating immune therapy and always build a steroid-sparing maintenance plan.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis and IBD guidance

title: IBS: Make a Positive Diagnosis Without Missing Alarm Disease
bottomLine: IBS is a positive symptom-based diagnosis after alarm features and a limited set of appropriate mimics are addressed. Do not subject low-risk patients to repeated broad testing, but do not use the IBS label to dismiss bleeding, weight loss, anemia, nocturnal symptoms or a major pattern change.
recognize: Recurrent abdominal pain related to defecation and change in stool frequency/form is characteristic; constipation-, diarrhea- and mixed-predominant phenotypes guide therapy.
Symptoms can fluctuate with meals, stress and other gut-brain factors without implying they are imaginary.
differentiate: Celiac disease should be considered/tested in appropriate patients; IBD, microscopic colitis, bile acid diarrhea, infection and colorectal disease enter the differential according to phenotype/risk.
Routine food-allergy panels, CRP/calprotectin or colonoscopy are not required for every uncomplicated IBS presentation.
assessment: Assess Rome-pattern symptoms, stool phenotype, duration, bleeding, weight loss, nocturnal symptoms, family history, medication/diet triggers, anxiety/depression and prior tests.
workup: Use targeted celiac testing and other investigations based on diarrhea phenotype/alarm features; avoid repetitive broad testing once a stable low-risk positive diagnosis is established.
management: Use individualized diet strategies such as a dietitian-guided low-FODMAP trial when appropriate, soluble fibre/psyllium, psychological gut-brain therapies and phenotype-specific medications.
Avoid overrestrictive long-term diets without reintroduction/nutritional support.
medicationSafety: Match constipation/diarrhea drugs to phenotype and contraindications; avoid chronic opioids because they can worsen bowel dysfunction and pain.
redFlags: New onset/pattern change at higher cancer risk
counselling: Validate IBS as a real disorder of gut-brain interaction and explain that a focused workup is safer than endless testing when alarm features are absent.
followUp: Track function and symptom burden; revisit diagnosis when alarm features or a significant phenotype change develops.
examTrap: Ordering repeated colonoscopy/food-allergy panels in stable low-risk IBS—or ignoring new rectal bleeding because the patient already carries an IBS label.
oneLinePearl: IBS is diagnosed positively, not by exhausting every possible test and not by ignoring future red flags.
sourceBasis: Canadian Association of Gastroenterology Clinical Practice Guideline for IBS

title: Viral Hepatitis B and C: Identify Active Infection, Stage Liver Risk, Link to Effective Therapy
bottomLine: HBV and HCV require different serologic/virologic interpretation. For HCV, a reactive antibody does not prove current infection—RNA confirms active infection and modern direct-acting antivirals cure most patients. For HBV, interpret surface antigen/antibodies/core antibody and HBV DNA/ALT phase together, then decide treatment and hepatocellular-carcinoma surveillance risk.
recognize: Chronic viral hepatitis is often asymptomatic until advanced disease; elevated liver tests may be mild or intermittent.
Pregnancy, immunosuppression, cirrhosis and coinfection change treatment/monitoring urgency.
differentiate: HCV antibody remains positive after spontaneous or treatment cure and requires RNA to distinguish current from resolved infection.
HBV surface antigen positivity, anti-HBc and anti-HBs patterns distinguish current, resolved, vaccine immunity and susceptibility; isolated results require clinical interpretation.
assessment: Assess blood/injection/sexual/perinatal exposure, country of origin/travel, alcohol, pregnancy, immunosuppression, prior antiviral treatment, family HCC history and decompensation symptoms.
workup: For HCV, confirm active infection with RNA and stage fibrosis/coinfections before treatment; current Canadian guidance supports treatment consideration for chronic infection regardless of fibrosis stage.
For HBV, use HBsAg/anti-HBc/anti-HBs, HBV DNA, ALT and fibrosis/coinfection context; use current CASL/AMMI guidance for treatment and surveillance thresholds.
management: Link HCV-positive RNA patients to DAA therapy and confirm sustained virologic response; assess reinfection risk because cure does not create immunity.
Use potent HBV nucleos(t)ide therapy or other specialist-guided management when current phase/risk criteria support treatment and prevent HBV reactivation during immunosuppression.
medicationSafety: Check DAA interactions carefully and renal/hepatic context; decompensated cirrhosis changes regimen options.
Stopping HBV therapy can cause flare and must follow specialist/current-guideline criteria rather than an arbitrary treatment duration.
redFlags: Pregnancy with high HBV transmission risk
counselling: Teach HCV cure versus reinfection, HBV household/sexual vaccination/testing and harm-reduction strategies without stigma.
followUp: Confirm HCV cure and maintain cirrhosis surveillance when indicated; for HBV track virology/ALT and HCC risk according to current Canadian guidance.
examTrap: Diagnosing active hepatitis C from antibody alone or assuming successful HCV treatment removes cirrhosis-related HCC surveillance needs.
oneLinePearl: HCV antibody tells you exposure; RNA tells you active virus. HBV requires the whole serologic/virologic pattern.
sourceBasis: PHAC Hepatitis C resources updated December 2025
